lesson.title: The Rules of Engagement Between Species
lesson.summary: Interspecific interactions, the ways different species affect each other's survival and reproduction within a community, can be classified by whether each participant is helped, harmed, or unaffected, covering competition, predation, herbivory, parasitism, mutualism, and commensalism.
lesson.body:
Within any ecological community, populations of different species are constantly affecting one another, sometimes helping, sometimes harming, sometimes with no effect at all. These are called interspecific interactions, interactions between individuals of different species, as distinct from intraspecific interactions like the within-species competition already discussed in the context of density dependence. A useful way to organize the major types of interspecific interaction is to note the effect on each participant using a simple plus, minus, or zero notation: does an interaction help a species (+), harm it (-), or leave it roughly unaffected (0)?

Competition is a minus-minus interaction: two species that rely on the same limited resource, whether that is food, light, nesting space, or something else, both do worse because the other is drawing down the shared supply. When two species compete for an identical limiting resource in an identical way, one classic ecological principle, sometimes called competitive exclusion, holds that they generally cannot coexist indefinitely: whichever species is even a slightly better competitor for that resource will tend to drive the other toward local extinction or force it to shift to a different resource or habitat over time. This idea traces back to laboratory experiments, including further work by G. F. Gause, the same researcher behind the density-dependent Paramecium experiments mentioned earlier, who found that when two Paramecium species relying on the same food source were grown together in a single culture, one consistently outcompeted and eliminated the other, while both survived fine when grown separately.

Predation and herbivory are both plus-minus interactions, one species benefits by consuming another, which is harmed or killed in the process, but each is distinctive enough, and common enough, to deserve its own dedicated discussion, which the next two chapters provide.

Parasitism is also plus-minus: a parasite lives on or inside a host, drawing resources from it and typically harming it, but usually without killing it quickly, since a parasite's own success generally depends on its host surviving long enough to keep supporting it. This distinguishes typical parasitism from typical predation, where the prey is killed outright.

Mutualism is a plus-plus interaction, both species benefit. A widely recognized example is pollination: a bee visiting a flower gains nectar or pollen as food, while the plant gains pollen transfer that enables it to reproduce. Mycorrhizal fungi living in association with plant roots are another well documented example: the fungi receive sugars produced by the plant, while the plant gains improved access to water and soil nutrients through the fungal network.

Commensalism is a plus-zero interaction, one species benefits while the other is largely unaffected. Barnacles attaching to a whale's skin are a commonly cited example: the barnacles gain a mobile platform that carries them through nutrient rich waters, while the whale is generally considered to experience little meaningful cost or benefit from their presence.

It is worth being cautious about treating these categories as fixed labels. The same pair of species can sometimes shift from one category to another depending on conditions, an interaction that functions as mutualism when resources are abundant might tip toward parasitism when they become scarce, for example. Even so, this framework of interaction types gives community ecology a shared vocabulary for describing how species shape each other's fates, which is exactly what the next two chapters put to use in exploring predation and herbivory in more depth.
